name: I had a bad experience with a contractor before—how can I protect myself on a seismic retrofit project this time?

mainEntity.name: I had a bad experience with a contractor before—how can I protect myself on a seismic retrofit project this time?

acceptedAnswer.text:
To protect yourself, focus on clear contracts, verified credentials, and strong oversight. Seismic retrofitting is technical, so you need both competent professionals and solid paperwork.

Use detailed, written agreements that tie payments to milestones and inspections, not vague promises. Consider keeping the engineer involved during construction to verify that work matches the design.

Key factors:
- Verify licenses, insurance, and references; avoid cash‑only deals
- Require detailed scope, drawings, and change‑order procedures in the contract
- Tie payment schedule to passed inspections and documented progress
- Keep written records of all decisions and field changes

Don’t rush into the lowest bid; instead, pick the contractor who best explains the project and is transparent about risks and unknowns. If something feels evasive during bidding, it rarely improves later.

A professional retrofit firm should welcome scrutiny and questions, not resist them.
acceptedAnswer.description: Protect yourself with verified licensing and insurance, a detailed written contract, and payment tied to clear milestones and inspections. Keep your engineer involved during construction and document all changes. Choose the contractor who is transparent and thorough, not just the cheapest or fastest talker.
